scenes.text: There is a very old idea, older than any of our religions, that every living thing already carries inside it the shape of what it is going to be.
The acorn does not know it is an oak.
It does not lie awake in the soil, worrying about whether it has the talent for it.
It does not read books about how to become a tree.
It simply becomes one, because that is what it is.
Now, you and I are a little more complicated than an acorn.
We are the only creatures, so far as we know, who can look at ourselves and ask, what am I supposed to be?
And that question is both our great gift and our great trouble.
Because the moment we ask it, we usually go looking for the answer in the wrong place.
We look outside.
We look at what our parents wanted, what our teachers praised, what the neighbours seem to admire.
We look at the people on the screens, the ones who seem to have arrived somewhere.
And we try to build ourselves out of borrowed pieces, like a house made from other people's furniture.
Then we wonder why we never quite feel at home in it.
The ancient Greek poet Pindar left behind a line that has echoed down for two and a half thousand years.
Become what you are.
Not become what you are told. Not become what you are afraid of. Become what you are.
It sounds simple. It is perhaps the hardest thing a human being can do.
And this is a talk about how it might be done.
Let us go back to the acorn for a moment, because it has more to teach us than we think.
Inside that small brown shell there is no tiny tree waiting to be unfolded, like a paper flower in water.
There is only a pattern, a tendency, a direction.
Whether it becomes a great oak depends on where it falls.
On rock, it withers. In shade, it waits. In good earth, with rain and light, it rises.
So becoming is never something you do alone.
It is a conversation between what is inside you and the world that surrounds you.
And here is the first thing most of us get wrong.
We think the seed must fight the soil.
We think that to become ourselves we must stand against everything, push, strain, grit our teeth and force our way upward.
But watch a tree grow, and you will see no strain in it at all.
Its roots go down exactly as far as they need to go. Its branches reach for the light that is actually there.
It does not grow toward the light it wishes it had.
There is a kind of intelligence in that.
Not the intelligence of planning, but the intelligence of response.
The tree listens to its world, and answers it, season after season.
And most of us have forgotten how to listen.
We were born listening.
A small child does not need to be told what is interesting to it.
It goes straight to the thing, the beetle, the puddle, the box of buttons, and it is completely absorbed.
Nobody has taught it to care about these things. It just does.
That absorption is the seed showing itself.
And then, slowly, the world begins to correct us.
Sit still. Be sensible. That is not a real job. People like us do not do that.
Every correction is a little fence put around the seedling.
Some fences are kind, and keep the young plant from being trampled.
But some of them are built by other people's fears, and they stay up long after the danger has passed.
By the time we are grown, many of us are living inside a garden of fences, and we call it our personality.
So the first step in becoming what you are is not to add anything.
It is to notice the fences.
To ask, gently, of each belief you hold about yourself, who put this here?
Did I choose it, or was it simply handed to me, the way you are handed a coat at the door?
You will be surprised how many of the walls in your life you never actually built.
The word person comes from an old Latin word, persona.
And a persona was the mask that an actor wore on the stage.
Think about that for a moment. The very word we use for who we are originally meant a mask.
Through the mouth of it, the sound of the actor's voice came out. Per sona. Through the sound.
Now, there is nothing wrong with masks.
You need a face for the office, a face for your family, a face for strangers on the train.
Society is a great play, and we all have parts in it.
The trouble begins when you forget that you are acting.
When the mask has been worn so long that it has grown into the skin.
When you go home at night, take off your shoes, sit alone in the quiet, and the mask is still on.
When you cannot remember what your own face looked like.
You can tell when this has happened, because life starts to feel like a performance with no interval.
You are tired, but not from work. You are tired from keeping the act going.
Every conversation becomes a small audition.
Every success feels like it belongs to someone else, because, in a sense, it does.
It belongs to the character you have been playing.
Here is the strange thing about all this.
We wear the mask because we are afraid that, without it, we would not be loved.
And yet the mask is exactly what keeps us from ever being loved.
Because when someone admires the mask, it is the mask they admire, not you.
So the more successful the performance, the lonelier the performer.
You see this in the lives of people who seem to have everything.
The great house, the reputation, the good marriage, all the outward signs of a life well built.
And inside it, a person quietly wondering when the real life is going to begin.
Waiting for permission to be the one they actually are.
Nobody is going to give you that permission.
Not because they are cruel, but because they cannot.
The only one who knows where the mask ends and the face begins is you.
And you find out the way an actor finds out, by stepping off the stage, now and then, and standing in the dark wings, where nobody is watching.
Just to feel what it is like to be no one in particular.
In ancient China, there is a story about a farmer who was worried that his rice was growing too slowly.
Every morning he went out and looked at the young shoots, and every morning they seemed exactly the same.
So one day, out of impatience, he went along the rows and pulled each shoot up a little, to help it grow.
He came home exhausted, and very pleased with himself. I have helped the rice to grow, he said.
His son ran out to the field to see. And every shoot was dead.
We do this to ourselves all the time.
We decide what we ought to be, and then we pull at ourselves to get there faster.
We read a book about discipline and wake at five o'clock for a week and then collapse.
We force ourselves into a career because it looks right on paper, and wonder why something in us goes quiet and grey.
We are trying to help the rice to grow.
The old Chinese sages had a word for the opposite of this. They called it wu wei.
It is usually translated as not doing, but that is not quite right.
It means not forcing. Acting in such a way that you go with the grain of things instead of against it.
A good carpenter does not hack at the wood. He feels where it wants to split, and he follows it.
A good sailor does not fight the wind. He uses it, even when it blows against him.
And a person who is becoming themselves does not fight their own nature.
They find where it is already moving, and they help it along.
So how do you find the grain of your own wood?
You look at where your attention goes when nobody is directing it.
What do you find yourself doing when you have an empty afternoon and nothing that must be done?
What could you talk about for hours, until you look up and the tea has gone cold?
What kind of difficulty do you not mind?
Because every life worth living has difficulty in it. The question is only which difficulty is yours.
Some people love the slow puzzle of numbers. Some love the mess of a kitchen. Some love standing in front of a room and making people laugh.
None of these is better than the others. They are simply different grains in different woods.
And here is the thing about the flower.
A rose does not try to be a lily.
It does not compare its petals with the tulip's and feel ashamed.
It has no idea that it is supposed to be beautiful. It just opens.
And the opening happens at its own speed, and no amount of shouting at it will make it open faster.
You cannot force a flower. You can only give it the light.
There is a woman who spent many years working as a nurse with people in the last weeks of their lives.
She sat with them, and listened, and over time she noticed that they kept saying the same things.
And the regret she heard more than any other was this.
I wish I had had the courage to live a life true to myself, and not the life others expected of me.
Not, I wish I had been richer. Not, I wish I had been more famous.
I wish I had been myself.
That is a terrible thing to discover at the end.
And the strange thing is that almost nobody who says it was ever forbidden to be themselves.
There was no law against it. No one locked the door.
They simply kept postponing it.
First, I will get settled. Then, when the children are grown. Then, when I retire.
And the years go by like a train you keep meaning to catch.
We do this because we imagine that life is a kind of rehearsal.
That the real performance is coming later, once everything is ready.
But there is no later. There is only this, now, happening.
This is the performance. The curtain has been up the whole time.
Now, I am not saying you should throw away your job tomorrow and run off to paint in the mountains.
Becoming yourself is rarely so dramatic.
More often it happens in small, almost invisible choices.
Saying no to the thing you do not want, even when it would be easier to say yes.
Saying yes to the thing that frightens you a little, but calls to you anyway.
Taking one evening a week for the work you love, even if nobody pays you for it.
Telling one person the truth about what you feel.
These small choices are like the first drops of rain on a dry hillside.
One drop does nothing. But they find each other, and gather into little streams.
And one day, without anyone noticing quite when, there is a river.
So do not wait until you are lying in a quiet room at the end of your days to discover who you were.
Find out now, while there is still time to live it.
Now, I do not want to make this sound easy, as if becoming yourself is just a matter of relaxing in the garden.
Because there is a part of it that hurts.
Think of the caterpillar.
At a certain point in its life, it stops eating, hangs itself from a branch, and wraps itself in a case of its own making.
And inside that case, something extraordinary happens.
It does not simply grow wings. It dissolves.
Almost the whole body of the caterpillar breaks down into a kind of soup.
And out of that soup, the butterfly is built.
If the caterpillar could think, I imagine it would be terrified.
Everything it knew itself to be is coming apart.
It would have no way of knowing that this was not death, but transformation.
Many of the most painful times in a human life are like this.
The end of a relationship. The loss of a job you thought defined you. A move to a strange city. An illness. A grief.
At the time, they feel like everything is falling apart. And in a sense, it is.
The old shape of you is dissolving.
But it is very often in exactly these moments that the new shape begins to form.
The sculptor Michelangelo is said to have described his work in a very simple way.
The statue is already inside the block of marble. I only take away what is not the statue.
Every blow of the chisel is a loss. A piece of stone, which was once part of the block, falls to the floor and is swept away.
If the stone could feel, it might grieve for every chip.
But without those losses, there would only ever be a block. Never a figure.
So when life takes something from you, it is worth asking a strange question.
Not only, why is this happening to me, but, what is being uncovered?
What part of me was hidden under the thing I have just lost?
This is not to say that suffering is good, or that you should go looking for it.
Only that, when it comes, as it comes to everyone, it does not have to be wasted.
There is a phrase from the German poet Rilke that I have always loved.
He wrote to a young poet who was in despair, and he told him, be patient toward all that is unsolved in your heart.
Try to love the questions themselves.
Live the questions now, and perhaps, without noticing it, you will gradually live along some distant day into the answer.
Lao Tzu, the old master of the Tao, said that the highest good is like water.
Water does not argue with anything.
It does not push against the rock in its path. It goes around it, or under it, or it waits until it has risen high enough to go over it.
And yet, given enough time, it wears the rock away.
Nothing in the world is softer than water, Lao Tzu said, and yet nothing is better at overcoming the hard and the strong.
There is a great lesson in this for anyone who wants to become something.
We imagine that becoming great requires a kind of violence. Hard work, hard discipline, a hard heart.
And there is a place for effort, of course. Water flows a long way.
But notice that it never stops being water.
It never tries to become stone in order to beat the stone.
When you try to become yourself by becoming hard, you usually become someone else.
You become the hardened version of yourself, the one who has no time, no softness, no play.
And then, when you arrive at the top of the mountain, you find you have lost the very person who wanted to climb it.
Water also teaches us something about stillness.
When a pond is churned up, you cannot see the bottom. The mud swirls everywhere.
But if you leave it alone, and do nothing at all, the mud settles by itself.
And the water becomes clear.
Most of us are trying to see who we are while constantly stirring the water.
We fill every quiet moment with noise, with news, with the endless chatter of other people's lives.
And then we complain that we do not know what we want.
Of course we don't. The water never gets the chance to settle.
So sit, sometimes, and do nothing at all.
Not as a technique, not to become more productive, but simply to let the mud fall.
Walk without headphones. Look out of a window for a long time.
And in that stillness, quietly, like a fish rising to the surface, something will come up.
A memory, a longing, a small and obvious truth you have been too busy to hear.
That is your nature, speaking. It has been speaking all along.
There is an old Indian story about a tiger cub who was raised by goats.
His mother had died, and the goats took him in, and so he grew up eating grass and bleating like them.
He was a rather poor goat. The grass made him thin, and his bleat came out strange.
One day an old tiger came out of the jungle, and the goats scattered, but the young one stood there, confused.
The old tiger looked at him in disgust and said, what are you doing, living among the goats?
And he took the cub by the scruff of the neck down to a still pool, and said, look.
And for the first time, the cub saw his own face in the water.
Then the old tiger gave him a piece of meat. The cub choked on it at first. And then something woke in him.
He opened his mouth, and out came, not a bleat, but a roar.
We are all, in some way, tigers who have been raised by goats.
Not because the goats were bad. They were only doing what goats do.
They taught us to be careful, to eat the grass, to stay with the herd.
And there is nothing wrong with any of that, if you are a goat.
But somewhere in you there may be a roar you have never let out.
A thing you have always wanted to make. A place you have always wanted to go. A way of living you have never dared to try.
And the strange thing is that it will not feel like becoming someone new.
It will feel like coming home.
This is what Pindar meant, and what Nietzsche meant when he took up the same words, become who you are.
You are not a project to be completed.
You are not a problem to be fixed.
You are more like a piece of music that is still being played.
And the point of music is not to get to the end of it. Otherwise the best composers would write only finales.
The point is the playing.
So, if you want to become what you are meant to become, here is perhaps all the advice there is.
Notice the fences that other people built in you, and take down the ones you do not need.
Wear your masks lightly, and never forget the face beneath them.
Do not pull at the rice. Find the grain of your own wood, and go with it.
When life breaks you open, ask what is being uncovered.
Be like water. Soft, patient, and impossible to stop.
Let the mud settle, and listen.
And when you finally see your own face in the pool, do not be afraid of the roar.
The acorn does not try to become an oak.
It only stops pretending to be anything else.
And in the end, after all the seasons, all the storms and all the patient years, there it stands.
Not a copy of any other tree in the forest.
Exactly what it was always meant to be.
You are already that.
Now become it.
